problem: VLN agents rely on expert trajectories or on augmentation and online exploration, which are costly and risky, while large repositories of suboptimal offline trajectories go unused. Standard offline-RL conditioning (e.g., returns-to-go) needs goal or return information that is unavailable at test time in VLN.
motivation: Scaling VLN data without online exploration matters for safety-critical real-world deployment. Suboptimal logged trajectories are cheap, but naive behavior cloning on them degrades performance. The paper's observation is that conditioning on a per-step progress signal lets the model separate good from bad actions during training, and be asked for progress-making actions at test time.
key_idea: Condition a VLN policy on a scale-agnostic reward token (the sign of the change in Euclidean distance to the goal between consecutive states) during training, and at test time feed a constant +1 (0 near the goal) to request goal-approaching actions.
insight: The reward token labels each demonstrated action as progress-making, regressive, or neutral, so suboptimal actions become 'explainable' rather than harmful, and asking for +1 at test time selects the good behavior. The sparse (sign) token beats the dense one because training then matches the test-time conditioning (scale mismatch is avoided; Table 1 sparse > dense mostly). The gains grow with noise (e.g., R2R Random dataset SR 20.48 -> 60.66), and returns-to-go conditioning fails on RxR because trajectory lengths vary widely. Analyses on 'tough' RxR subsets with goal deviations show the greedy token still helps.
method: Reward token (dense): δD = D(s_t,G) - D(s_{t+1},G), the Euclidean change in distance to the goal, computed from training trajectories using the goal coordinates.
Reward token (sparse): sign of δD in {+1,-1,0}, which is scale-agnostic and used as the main variant.
Test-time conditioning: a fixed +1 at every step and 0 when the agent detects it is at the goal, with no goal coordinates or next-state prediction needed.

Conditioning mechanism in VLN↻BERT: add the token to the recurrent state token before each cross-attention and self-attention block. The alternative, concatenation with a projected embedding, performs similarly. In MTVM the token is added to the [CLS] embedding.

VLN-ORL benchmark: HAMT rollouts on R2R/RxR train instructions, perturbed with random-action noise (0%, 15%, 30%, 100% random) plus a Mixture (expert + 15% noisy), and trained with cross-entropy on the logged actions.
Return-conditioned baseline: returns-to-go token = distance to goal in training; at test time initialized to the max validation trajectory length and decremented by distance traveled.

setting.backbone: VLN↻BERT and MTVM (trained from scratch, reward-conditioned)
setting.training_data: Offline datasets generated by rolling out a pretrained HAMT on R2R train (14,025 instructions) and RxR English train (26,464 pairs), with noise variants (Expert, 15%, 30%, Mixture, Random); no pretraining or augmentation.
setting.observation: Panoramic RGB (36 views, ResNet-152 Places365 features) with language instruction
setting.privileged: Training: goal and agent coordinates for reward computation. Test: the agent is assumed to detect goal completion (stop signal); episode terminated at goal for baselines too.

numbers.extra: trained offline on HAMT-generated Expert data; assumes goal-completion detection

numbers_note: Only the HAMT-rollout offline benchmark is used; results are not comparable to standard R2R/RxR leaderboards. Test splits are not reported. The RxR val-seen numbers and other noise levels are in Table 1 but were not all listed.
results: Reward-conditioned VLN↻BERT beats plain VLN↻BERT and the return-conditioned variant on nearly all datasets. For example, on the R2R val-unseen Expert set SR is 67.09 vs 54.92 for the baseline, and on Random SR is 60.66 vs 20.48. Gains are larger with more noise, and they also appear for MTVM (Random SR 58.32 vs 33.33 on val-unseen). Navigation error and trajectory length are sometimes worse.
limitations: Requires prior knowledge of the stop/goal state at test time (goal-completion detection) to terminate episodes.
The greedy progress token may lengthen paths and raise NE, and performance drops on trajectories with many consecutive goal deviations.
Datasets are synthetic (HAMT rollouts with random-action noise), so real suboptimal data is not tested; results are val-only and not comparable to standard VLN leaderboards.
